chunks: "In principle you integrate the acceleration once to get velocity and again to get position. In practice you cannot do that for long, and the reasons are what matter.
First, an accelerometer measures specific force, so gravity is in the signal.
To remove it I need to know the orientation of the sensor, which means rotating the readings into a world frame using a gyro-based attitude estimate and then subtracting 1 g on the vertical axis.
Any error in the attitude leaks gravity into the horizontal axes: a 0. 1 degree tilt error is 0.
017 metres per second squared, which doubly integrated is about 31 metres after a minute. Second, any bias gets integrated twice.
A bias b gives velocity b times t and position one half b t squared, so even a 1 milli-g bias, which is a good consumer part, is 0.
5 metres after 10 seconds and 18 metres after a minute. Noise integrates too, but as a random walk, which is usually smaller than the bias term.
So with a consumer IMU position is only usable for a second or a few seconds.

To make it useful, I apply corrections: reset velocity to zero when I know the device is stationary, which is called a zero-velocity update, calibrate bias, and fuse with GPS, a camera, wheel odometry or LiDAR, which give absolute or drift-free position."
